messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Samir, a 40-year-old software engineer living with his wife in a suburban apartment complex, had always thought of himself as a steady, practical person—someone who solved problems by thinking them through. That changed one late autumn evening when a moderate earthquake, far stronger than anything the region had experienced in decades, struck without warning. He had been at his desk, writing code, when the floor began to shudder and the walls groaned. For twenty seconds that felt like hours, the building swayed, ceiling tiles fell, and glass shattered from a framed photograph on his desk. What stayed with him most vividly, even now, was the sound: a low, grinding roar from the earth beneath the foundation, mixed with the high-pitched screech of twisting metal and the panicked shouts of his neighbor in the next apartment. He could not later say in what order these things happened—the memory came as a jumble of images and sensations that he could never assemble into a clear timeline. When a memory surfaced, it arrived not as a recollection but as a full reliving: he would feel the tremor in his legs, smell the dust and ozone, hear the screech again, and his heart would race as if the ground were still moving.

In the weeks after the earthquake, Samir found himself unable to let the memory settle. At first he tried to force himself to think only positive thoughts—the building had held, he was alive, his wife was safe—but the command felt hollow, and the intrusive images broke through within minutes. He also noticed a growing, bitter obsession. The earthquake had been a natural disaster, but in his mind it had an author: the property management company that had neglected structural upgrades, the city inspectors who had signed off. He spent hours ruminating about how to get even with those he held responsible, drafting imaginary legal complaints and dwelling on vengeance scenarios even as he knew it made no sense. The anger gave him a strange energy, but it also kept the event fresh.

Samir’s environment became laced with triggers. At the office, if a colleague approached his cubicle unexpectedly, he would flinch, his hands shooting up defensively. When someone tapped his shoulder to get his attention, he would whirl around, heart pounding, before he could identify the person. He began to map every room he entered for escape routes—where the exits were, whether a door opened inward or outward, whether the windows could be forced. He did this unconsciously now. His work as a software engineer required long hours in an open-plan office, but he had started choosing a desk against the wall, facing the door, and could not concentrate unless he had a clear path to the stairwell.

The negative appraisals took root quietly. He would think, *Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation*—he should have checked the building’s seismic rating, should have moved to a safer area. Then the thought would spiral: *Nothing good can happen to me anymore.* Before the earthquake, Samir had been an easygoing, optimistic man. Now, he told himself he used to be happy but was always miserable. His wife noticed the change; he was irritable, withdrawn, and refused to go near the hospital where they had gone for treatment of minor cuts from the debris. When she suggested a routine physical, he snapped, “I don’t need a doctor.” He had come to believe that any medical setting—the sounds of gurneys, the antiseptic smell, the sight of an ambulance—would throw him back into the terror. He rerouted his drive home to avoid the medical center.

Months passed. Samir’s avoidance narrowed his life. He stopped attending the weekly team outings his colleagues organized, afraid of the crowded, unfamiliar restaurants where he could not quickly find an exit. His wife grew distant, hurt by his refusal to talk about the earthquake and his sharp reactions to her touch. It was only when she told him, gently but firmly, that she could not keep living like this that he agreed to come for help. What frightened Samir most was the possibility that talking about the earthquake would break something inside him permanently—that the memories would overwhelm him and he would never put the pieces back in order. But he also hoped, with a small, tired part of himself, that somewhere in that conversation he might find the sequence he had lost, and a way to feel safe in his own skin again.
